SECTIONS.title: How do we measure velocity?
ideas: A position function $s(t)$ tells where an object is at time $t$. Average velocity over $[a,b]$ is the change in position divided by the change in time, which is the slope of the secant line through $(a,s(a))$ and $(b,s(b))$.
Instantaneous velocity at $t=a$ is what average velocity approaches as the interval $[a,a+h]$ shrinks ($h\to0$). Numerically: compute $AV_{[a,a+h]}$ for smaller and smaller $h$ on both sides of $a$.
Units of a rate are always $\dfrac{\text{units of output}}{\text{units of input}}$, e.g. feet per second, dollars per year, mg per hour.
On a graph: average rate $=$ slope of a secant; instantaneous rate $=$ slope of the tangent.

SECTIONS.title: The notion of limit
ideas: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$ means $f(x)$ can be made as close to $L$ as we like by taking $x$ close enough to $a$ (but $x\neq a$). The value $f(a)$ is irrelevant: it may not exist, or may differ from $L$.
The limit exists exactly when the left-hand limit $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)$ and right-hand limit $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$ both exist and are equal.

Three kinds of "plug-in" outcomes. If substituting gives $\frac{c}{d}$ with $d\neq0$: that is the limit (a valid answer). If it gives $\frac{c}{0}$ with $c\neq0$: vertical asymptote, the limit does not exist (it blows up to $\pm\infty$). If it gives $\frac{0}{0}$: indeterminate form, do more algebra.
Algebra tools for $\frac00$: factor and cancel; multiply by a conjugate; combine fractions with a common denominator.
Estimate limits from a table (approach from both sides) or a graph (follow the curve toward $x=a$ from each side).

SECTIONS.title: The derivative of a function at a point
ideas: The derivative of $f$ at $x=a$ is the limit of average rates of change over $[a,a+h]$ as $h\to0$. It is the slope of the tangent line at $(a,f(a))$ and the instantaneous rate of change of $f$ at $a$.
Equivalent form: $f'(a) = \lim_{x\to a}\dfrac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}$.
Graphically, estimate $f'(a)$ by drawing the tangent line at $(a,f(a))$ and reading its rise over run.
Working the limit definition always follows the same rhythm: write $f(a+h)$, subtract $f(a)$, simplify until every remaining term has a factor of $h$, cancel the $h$, then let $h\to0$.

SECTIONS.title: The derivative function
ideas: Letting the point vary gives a new function $f'(x)$, the derivative function: $f'(x) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
Reading $f'$ from the graph of $f$: where $f$ rises, $f'>0$; where $f$ falls, $f'<0$; at a peak or valley (smooth), $f'=0$; at a corner or cusp, $f'$ is undefined; steeper $f$ means larger $|f'|$.
Sketching $f'$: mark the zeros first (where $f$ has horizontal tangents), decide the sign on each interval, then estimate steepness.
Notation: $f'(x)$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}[f(x)]$, $y'$.

SECTIONS.title: Interpreting, estimating, and using the derivative
ideas: Units: $f'(a)$ has units of $f$ per unit of $x$. If $M(t)$ is mg at $t$ hours, $M'(t)$ is mg per hour.

The interpretation sentence. "$f'(a)=c$" means: when the input is $a$ (units), the output is changing at a rate of $c$ (units of $f$ per unit of $x$). Include: the input value with units, the direction (increasing/decreasing), the rate with units.
Estimating from data: use a difference quotient. Central difference (averaging both neighbors) is usually the best estimate when data on both sides is available.
Using the derivative: for small $h$, $f(a+h)\approx f(a) + f'(a)\,h$ (a step along the tangent line).

SECTIONS.title: The second derivative
ideas: $f''$ is the derivative of $f'$: it measures how the rate of change is changing. In motion, $s'$ is velocity and $s''$ is acceleration.

$f'>0$: $f$ increasing. $f'<0$: $f$ decreasing. $f''>0$: $f'$ increasing, so $f$ is concave up (bends like $\cup$). $f''<0$: $f$ is concave down ($\cap$). An inflection point is where concavity changes.
Language: "increasing at an increasing rate" means $f'>0$ and $f''>0$; "decreasing at a decreasing rate" (decreasing more slowly) means $f'<0$ and $f''>0$.
From a graph of $f'$: $f$ is increasing where $f'$ is above the axis; $f$ is concave up where $f'$ is rising.

SECTIONS.title: Limits, continuity, and differentiability
ideas: $f$ is continuous at $a$ when three things hold: $f(a)$ is defined, $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists, and they are equal. Informally: no hole, no jump, no vertical asymptote at $a$.
Discontinuities: removable (hole), jump (one-sided limits differ), infinite (vertical asymptote).
$f$ is differentiable at $a$ when $f'(a)$ exists (the difference-quotient limit). Not differentiable at a corner, a cusp, a vertical tangent, or any discontinuity.
Differentiable $\Rightarrow$ continuous. The converse is false: $|x|$ is continuous but not differentiable at $0$.
To make a piecewise function continuous at the break, set the two one-sided limits equal and solve for the unknown constant.

SECTIONS.title: The tangent line approximation
ideas: The tangent line (linearization) at $a$ is $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$. Near $a$, $f(x)\approx L(x)$ because differentiable functions are locally linear.
Concavity tells you the error's sign: if $f$ is concave up near $a$, the tangent line lies below the curve, so $L(x)$ underestimates $f(x)$. Concave down: overestimate.
Farther from $a$ means a worse approximation.

SECTIONS.title: Elementary derivative rules
ideas: Constant, power, constant-multiple and sum/difference rules let you differentiate any polynomial term by term. The power rule works for any real exponent, so rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: $\sqrt{x}=x^{1/2}$, $\frac1{x^3} = x^{-3}$.
Exponentials: $\frac{d}{dx}[e^x]=e^x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}[a^x] = a^x\ln a$. Note $e^x$ is its own derivative; $x^e$ uses the power rule.
Derivatives of sums are sums of derivatives, but derivatives of products are not products of derivatives (see §2.3).

SECTIONS.title: Sine and cosine
ideas: $\frac{d}{dx}[\sin x] = \cos x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}[\cos x] = -\sin x$. These are true when $x$ is in radians.
Remember the cycle: $\sin \to \cos \to -\sin \to -\cos \to \sin$.
Know the unit-circle values at $0,\ \frac\pi6,\ \frac\pi4,\ \frac\pi3,\ \frac\pi2,\ \pi$ so you can evaluate $f'$ at specific points without a calculator.

SECTIONS.title: Product and quotient rules
ideas: Product rule: derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times derivative of the second.
Quotient rule: "low d-high minus high d-low, over the square of what's below." The order in the numerator matters.
If a quotient has a constant denominator, or the numerator is a constant times a power, simplify first: $\frac{x^3}{5} = \frac15 x^3$, $\frac{4}{x^2} = 4x^{-2}$.

SECTIONS.title: Derivatives of other trigonometric functions
ideas: All four come from the quotient rule applied to $\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, $\cot x = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$, $\sec x = \frac1{\cos x}$, $\csc x = \frac1{\sin x}$.
Pattern: every "co" function has a negative derivative.

SECTIONS.title: The chain rule
ideas: For a composite $f(g(x))$: differentiate the outside function, evaluate it at the inside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
Spot the inside function: anything "wrapped" in a power, root, exponential, log or trig function. $e^{3x^2}$ has inside $3x^2$; $(x^2+1)^5$ has inside $x^2+1$; $\sin(\cos x)$ has inside $\cos x$.
Chain rule combines with every other rule: $\frac{d}{dx}[x^2 e^{5x}] = 2xe^{5x} + 5x^2e^{5x}$ (product rule with a chain inside).

SECTIONS.title: Derivatives of inverse functions
ideas: If $f$ has inverse $f^{-1}$, then $(f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'\big(f^{-1}(x)\big)}$. The slope of the inverse at $(b,a)$ is the reciprocal of the slope of $f$ at $(a,b)$.
This produces the derivatives of $\ln x$ (inverse of $e^x$), $\log_b x$, $\arcsin x$, $\arctan x$, $\arccos x$.
With the chain rule: $\frac{d}{dx}[\ln(u)] = \frac{u'}{u}$, $\frac{d}{dx}[\arctan(u)] = \frac{u'}{1+u^2}$.

SECTIONS.title: Implicit differentiation
ideas: When $y$ is defined by an equation like $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ rather than a formula $y = f(x)$, differentiate both sides with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a function of $x$: every $y$-term picks up a factor $\frac{dy}{dx}$ by the chain rule.
Then collect the $\frac{dy}{dx}$ terms on one side and solve. The answer usually involves both $x$ and $y$; to find a slope at a point, substitute both coordinates.
Product terms like $xy$ need the product rule: $\frac{d}{dx}[xy] = y + x\frac{dy}{dx}$.

SECTIONS.title: L'Hôpital's rule and limits at infinity
ideas: L'Hôpital: if $\lim \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ has the form $\frac00$ or $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$, then it equals $\lim\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$ (when that limit exists). Differentiate top and bottom separately, not with the quotient rule. Always verify the form first.

Limits at infinity describe end behaviour and horizontal asymptotes. For rational functions compare degrees: numerator lower $\to 0$; equal $\to$ ratio of leading coefficients; numerator higher $\to \pm\infty$.
Dominating terms: as $x\to\infty$, exponentials $e^{x}$ beat powers $x^n$, which beat logarithms $\ln x$. E.g. $\frac{x^{100}}{e^x}\to0$ and $\frac{\ln x}{\sqrt x}\to0$.

SECTIONS.title: Using derivatives to identify extreme values
ideas: A critical number $c$ is a point in the domain where $f'(c)=0$ or $f'(c)$ is undefined. Local extrema of a continuous function can only occur at critical numbers (but not every critical number is an extremum).
First derivative test: if $f'$ changes from $+$ to $-$ at $c$, local max; from $-$ to $+$, local min; no sign change, neither.
Second derivative test: if $f'(c)=0$ and $f''(c)<0$, local max; $f''(c)>0$, local min; $f''(c)=0$, inconclusive (use the first derivative test).
Inflection points occur where $f''$ changes sign (candidates: $f''=0$ or undefined).

SECTIONS.title: Global optimization
ideas: Extreme Value Theorem: a continuous function on a closed interval $[a,b]$ attains an absolute maximum and minimum.
Closed interval method: find critical numbers in $(a,b)$, evaluate $f$ at those and at the endpoints $a$, $b$; the largest value is the absolute max, the smallest the absolute min.
On an open or infinite interval, use the shape of $f$ (sign of $f'$, limits at the ends) instead: a single critical number where $f'$ changes from $-$ to $+$ is a global min.

SECTIONS.title: Applied optimization
ideas: Procedure: draw a picture and name variables; write the quantity to optimize (objective); write the constraint; use the constraint to make the objective a function of one variable; state the domain; find critical numbers; check endpoints or use a derivative test; answer the actual question with units.
Classic set-ups: fencing a rectangle (perimeter constraint, area objective), open box from a sheet (cut corners), minimizing material for a can, shortest distance from a point to a curve.

SECTIONS.title: Related rates
ideas: Several quantities change with time and are linked by an equation. Differentiate that equation with respect to $t$ (implicitly), then substitute the known values and rates to find the unknown rate.

Steps: draw and label; list what is known (values and rates $\frac{d\square}{dt}$) and what is wanted; write the relating equation (geometry, Pythagoras, similar triangles, trig); differentiate with respect to $t$; substitute after differentiating; answer with units.
Do not plug in a value that changes with time until after you differentiate.

SECTIONS.title: Determining distance traveled from velocity
ideas: If velocity $v(t)\ge0$, the distance traveled on $[a,b]$ is the area under the velocity graph. For simple shapes (rectangles, triangles, trapezoids) compute geometrically.
When $v$ changes sign, area above the axis counts positive and below counts negative for net change in position; total distance adds the absolute areas.
Approximate irregular areas with rectangles: this is the seed of the Riemann sum.
Position is an antiderivative of velocity: if $s'=v$ then $s(b) - s(a) = $ net signed area under $v$.

SECTIONS.title: Riemann sums
ideas: Divide $[a,b]$ into $n$ pieces of width $\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}$ with endpoints $x_i = a + i\Delta x$. A Riemann sum adds up rectangle areas $f(x_i^*)\Delta x$ using a chosen sample point in each piece.
Left sum $L_n$ uses left endpoints, right sum $R_n$ uses right endpoints, midpoint sum $M_n$ uses midpoints. $M_n$ is usually most accurate.
If $f$ is increasing, $L_n$ underestimates and $R_n$ overestimates the area; if decreasing, the reverse.
Sigma notation: $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i)\Delta x$. As $n\to\infty$ all Riemann sums approach the definite integral.

SECTIONS.title: The definite integral
ideas: $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)\Delta x$: the net signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis on $[a,b]$.
Properties: linearity, splitting at a point, reversing limits changes the sign, $\int_a^a f = 0$.
Average value of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is $\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$: the height of the rectangle with the same area.
Use geometry (triangles, semicircles) to evaluate integrals of simple graphs exactly.

SECTIONS.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
ideas: FTC (evaluation): if $F' = f$ on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$. Any antiderivative works; the constant cancels.
Total change theorem: $\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = f(b) - f(a)$: integrating a rate gives the net change in the quantity.
You need a table of basic antiderivatives (reverse the derivative rules). Check by differentiating.

SECTIONS.title: Constructing accurate graphs of antiderivatives
ideas: If $F' = f$, then $F$ is increasing where $f>0$, decreasing where $f<0$, has local extrema where $f$ changes sign, and is concave up where $f$ is increasing.
The integral function $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ is the antiderivative of $f$ with $F(a)=0$; its values are net signed areas.
The indefinite integral $\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C$ is the whole family of antiderivatives.

SECTIONS.title: The second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
ideas: Second FTC: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_a^x f(t)\,dt = f(x)$. Differentiating an integral function returns the integrand evaluated at the upper limit.
With a variable upper limit $g(x)$, the chain rule applies: $\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{g(x)} f(t)\,dt = f(g(x))\,g'(x)$.
Every continuous function has an antiderivative, namely $\int_a^x f(t)dt$, even when no elementary formula exists (e.g. $\int_0^x e^{-t^2}dt$).
